# Soothing Sleep

> Soothing Sleep (YouTube @SleepSooth) publishes hour-long 3D nature sound videos for sleep and relaxation, runs the free Canopy & Tide browser sound mixer, and writes short evidence-based guides on sleep, rest, relaxation and sleepmaxxing.

## Guides
- [Sleepmaxxing: what actually works, and what to skip](https://sleepsooth.com/sleepmaxxing): Sleepmaxxing works when it focuses on the basics: a consistent sleep and wake time, 7 or more hours in bed asleep, a dark, cool and quiet bedroom, morning daylight, and no caffeine in the afternoon. Trendy extras such as mouth taping, sleep cocktails and chasing a perfect sleep score have weak evidence, and some carry risks.
- [White, pink and brown noise for sleep: which sound is best?](https://sleepsooth.com/sleep-sounds): The best sleep sound is a steady one you find easy to ignore. White noise is bright and hissy, pink noise is softer and balanced, and brown noise is deep and rumbly, like heavy rain or wind. Research suggests sound mainly helps by masking disruptive noise, and the evidence that it improves sleep overall is still limited.
- [How to relax before bed: a 20-minute wind-down](https://sleepsooth.com/relaxation): To relax before bed, give yourself 20 minutes of wind-down: dim the lights and put screens away, write tomorrow's to-do list, do a few minutes of slow breathing with a longer exhale, relax each muscle group in turn, and play a quiet, steady sound if it helps.

## Tools
- [Canopy & Tide](https://canopytide.com/): free 3D sleep sound mixer with rain, thunderstorm, ocean, forest, river, wind, light rain and Tibetan singing bowls, and a sleep timer.

## Quick facts
- Adults should sleep 7 or more hours a night (AASM and Sleep Research Society consensus, Watson et al. 2015).
- Continuous background noise mainly helps by masking disruptive sounds; overall evidence that it improves sleep is very low quality (Riedy et al. 2021).
- CBT-I is the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia (AASM guideline, Edinger et al. 2021).
- Mouth taping has weak evidence and possible risks (PLOS One systematic review, 2025).
